name: Tatra 87
hook: The first car across the Nubian Desert had no radiator at all — its V8 sat behind the back wheels, cooled by nothing but air.
story: On the morning of 22 April 1947, two young Czech engineers pulled away from an auto club in Prague in a silver saloon they had talked a factory into lending them. Jiří Hanzelka and Miroslav Zikmund were not explorers. They were economics graduates with a plan and a typewriter. Their car was a Tatra 87, and it looked like an odd choice for Africa: a V8 in the tail, a fin down its back, and no radiator to boil. That turned out to be the point. They crossed the Nubian Desert, reckoned to be the first to manage it by car, and the sand packing the cooling intakes was the worst of it. The engine never overheated. They reached Cape Town, shipped to South America, and drove home into Prague on 1 November 1950, three and a half years and 44 countries later. Their dispatches filled the papers. Their radio reports became the most popular programme in the country. The car is a national monument now.
description: The Tatra 87 was a streamlined luxury saloon built in Kopřivnice, Czechoslovakia, from 1936 to 1950. Hans Ledwinka and Erich Übelacker hung an air-cooled overhead-cam V8 behind the rear axle and wrapped it in a teardrop body with a dorsal fin to steady the long tail in crosswinds. Around 85 hp took it to nearly 100 mph on roughly 12.5 litres of fuel per 100 km. Some 3,056 were built. A 1979 wind-tunnel test measured its drag at 0.36.
